terms.grammar: verb, irregular: the passive of faciō
evidence: Cic. Fam. 16.21.7: rūsticus Rōmānus factus es
Hor. Ars 25–26: brevis esse labōrō, obscūrus fīō
terms.comment: With a noun or an adjective that agrees with the subject (obscūrus fīō). Quid mē fīet? is “what will become of me?”, with the ablative of the person, the dative or dē (Lewis & Short, s.v. faciō); ut fit is “as usually happens” (Liv. 3.1.7). Many changes of state have a verb of their own in -scō: jam advesperāscit, it’s getting dark (Ter. And. 581).

evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.126: quōs jūdicābat nōn posse ōrātōrēs ēvādere
terms.comment: Of how someone or something turns out in the end.

phrases.latin: sed quid Tulliolā meā fīet? jam id vōs vidēte; mihi deest cōnsilium.
phrases.english: but what will become of my little Tullia? You must see to that now; I am at a loss.

phrases.latin: dēpōnendae tibi sunt urbānitātēs; rūsticus Rōmānus factus es
phrases.english: you must put away your town manners: you have become a Roman countryman

phrases.latin: lēnior et melior fīs accēdente senectā?
phrases.english: are you growing gentler and better as old age comes on?

phrases.latin: opus rūsticum omne cūret utī sciat facere, et id faciat saepe, dum nē lassus fīat
phrases.english: let him see that he knows how to do all the farm work, and let him do it often, so long as he doesn’t get worn out
